prize_parts.citation: for developing methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets with endogenous prices, which made it possible to measure market power, merger effects and welfare empirically

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: B001 as a single achievement, credited to Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn. What I did in this round was test it against the chair's questions. My criterion for separating a measurement discovery from a toolkit has three parts. The method must (1) solve a problem that blocked inference, (2) produce counterfactuals that earlier approaches could not (substitution patterns, markups, merger and welfare effects), and (3) change practice and spread beyond its home field after long testing. BLP-type demand estimation meets all three. Endogenous prices and heterogeneous substitution were the obstacles, and the framework removed them. Merger review, antitrust and regulation use it routinely, and it has spread to trade, health and environmental economics. About three decades of use have exposed its weaknesses, and those are understood. The attribution is also the most compact on the shortlist. The central 1995 result is jointly authored by the trio, and Berry's inversion is part of it. I would keep the unit of the prize at demand estimation and market power. Dynamic-industry and production-function work would stay as supporting context. I would not try to credit every strand. I would also keep this to one achievement. A second achievement would need names outside the BLP trio and would exceed the three-person limit. It would also weaken a citation that is currently tight. The issue the Committee has to settle is the third name and how the citation is framed. I do not see an issue of readiness.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is still toolkit versus discovery, and the choice of third laureate comes right behind it. If the Committee wanted a programme-level citation on the new empirical IO, Bresnahan has a stronger claim than Levinsohn. A method-level citation excludes him, and that is a real cost. Applied BLP results are also sensitive to instrument choice, functional form and numerical implementation. That is documented, and it limits how much weight any single application can carry. I think the right response is to make the citation modest about this, but the sensitivities are not trivial. My alternatives have their own weaknesses. B009 overlaps with the 2024 institutions prize and has weaker cross-country identification. B002 overlaps with the 2022 prize and has an unresolved Gertler question. On the evidence in the exchange, neither is more mature or more cleanly attributable than B001.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first but names Bresnahan, not Levinsohn, as the third laureate. He argues that Bresnahan's new empirical IO and early differentiated-product demand work supplied the question the later tools answered. He accepts that a Levinsohn version would not be a scientific error.
responses.response: I still prefer Levinsohn, and I want to say what would change that. Under a method-level citation, Levinsohn is a co-author of the specific jointly authored result, and leaving him out splits the trio that defines the estimator. Under a programme-level citation on the new empirical IO, Bresnahan clearly belongs and I would accept the swap. But that is a different prize with a more diffuse credit boundary, and it would invite the wider claims of Reiss, Benkard and Levin. I do not think the Committee needs to adopt it to honour Bresnahan's role. My answer to the chair's framing question is that I support the method-level citation, I would accept Bresnahan only if the Committee deliberately chose the programme-level one, and I would then ask for the wording to be changed so that it does not credit the BLP paper itself. I do not regard the two versions as a merit difference. They are a choice about what is being rewarded.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, supports the BLP trio and defines the unit narrowly as demand and competition estimation plus the dynamic-industry framework. He warns that widening the citation to production-function and entry work would blur the prize and reopen attribution. He treats B002 as a clean Kiyotaki-Moore pair.
responses.response: I agree with the narrow unit, and it is the reason I would not follow the chair's wording into the dynamic-industry strand more than as context. Pakes anchors it, but the other two credited names do not, and a citation that claims it invites the question of Benkard, Levin and others. On the chair's question about sensitivities, my view comes from background knowledge and I have not verified it independently. What matters for merger and welfare conclusions is how robust the estimated own-price elasticities and implied markups are to instrument choice and functional form. Numerical convergence matters less once it is handled properly. I would want the citation to avoid overclaiming precision. I would be persuaded to lower B001 by documented cases in which reasonable instrument or specification choices reversed a merger or welfare conclusion. I would also be persuaded by a systematic replication study showing this. Our past co-authorship is disclosed below, and it does not change my view.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B013 first because it combines an explanatory framework with credible new empirical designs and large policy influence. She names B001 as the strongest alternative. She notes that committees weigh toolkits and discoveries differently, and says she cannot establish that as a merit gap.
responses.response: I respect the case for B013, and I agree with her on one point. First-place counts are not evidence of merit, and I do not rely on them. We differ on maturity and attribution. The skill-demand and China-shock strands have two different cores, and any three-name cap forces a choice between Katz and Dorn. The magnitudes and persistence of the local effects are still debated. For B001 the debate is about numerical and identification detail, and it was settled long ago on whether the method works. On toolkit versus discovery, I would say that the discovery in B001 is a measurement capability. It changed what can be known about substitution, markups and welfare. That is why I do not treat it as a lesser category than a substantive finding. I would revisit B013 if the Committee settled on a single strand with a clean trio. I would not rank it above B001 on the current exchange.

responses.point: Stromberg ranks B001 first. He raises the question of whether a second achievement could be added within the three-person limit, and he says the pooled entry makes the unit of the prize contestable.
responses.response: I considered a second achievement and I do not support it. With the BLP trio already using all three places, a second part would need names on both sides to be shared or dropped, which weakens the credit for each. A narrower BLP citation with no second part is easier to defend. His point about the pooled unit is the right one, and I think the answer is a citation that names demand estimation with endogenous prices and market power and stops there. I agree with him that B002, if the Committee turns to it, is cleaner as the Kiyotaki-Moore pair. I would keep B009 ahead of it among my alternatives only because I rank it higher. The Kiyotaki-Moore pair has come closer to B009 as a credible alternative during this exchange.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee prefers a method-level citation (Levinsohn as the third laureate) or a programme-level one (Bresnahan as the third laureate), and whether the choice reflects a difference in what is rewarded or a difference in merit.

Whether the Committee treats an estimation toolkit as a sufficient discovery. My criterion is changed practice, new counterfactuals and spread beyond the field. I recognise that others may weigh methods differently.

How far the sensitivity of applied BLP results to instruments, functional form and numerical implementation should temper the wording of the citation. This rests on my background knowledge and I have not independently verified it.
Whether the dynamic-industry work should be reflected in the citation if only Pakes of the three is credited for it.
I rely on background knowledge for citation, adoption and regulatory-use claims, and I have not independently verified any of them.
statement.conflict_note: Per my profile, I have no apparent tie to Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn. My field, industrial organisation and international trade, is close to B001, B050 and B021, and I have tried to apply the same criteria to every candidate. I ranked B050 eighth and B021 third in my opening, and neither is in my configuration. Disclosed, not adjudicated: I have co-authored with Committee colleagues John Hassler (the chair) and Tore Ellingsen (IJIO 2026). I am married to Magdalena Andersson, a Swedish politician. The profile gives no evidence that either bears on this prize. My listed co-authors, including Chad Syverson and Itay Goldstein, are not credited on any shortlisted entry. Hassler is also a B001 supporter, so our agreement on B001 should not be read as independent confirmation.
